rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark ruling by the top regional court and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The regional court ruled in 2024 that the country must recognise gender-identity changes made in other members of the regional bloc (a landmark case), and the national courts definitively confirmed this in March 2026. The annual Pride march marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (church leadership successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified and repeatedly used for political mobilisation.

For a visitor: part of a regional open-border zone, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. Under the regional court's ruling, identity documents issued elsewhere in the regional bloc must be recognised.
rewrites.blindTangential: No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The court-based domestic legal gender recognition regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the regional court's ruling directly benefits trans visitors whose identity documents were issued elsewhere in the regional bloc.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.
blindSourceSummaries: Note: the original report was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying report (Oct 2024) covers the regional court's ruling that the country infringed a transgender man's rights in a case on recognition of a foreign gender-recognition document.

A local rights organisation (31 Mar 2026): a city court ordered a new birth certificate for a trans man reflecting his foreign-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after a higher court rejected appeals filed by local civil-status offices — building on the regional court's 2024 ruling that member countries of the bloc must transcribe legal gender recognition performed elsewhere in the bloc. Announced on the international day of trans visibility; the organisation urges others who changed documents in another bloc country to pursue transcription in the nation.

A regional rights network's annual review (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — a candidate declared himself opposed to LGBTQ people in February and the prime minister mocked gender-marker changes; the national broadcasting regulator issued a public warning to a television channel in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after a rights-group complaint; a local deputy mayor made further derogatory announcements.

A regional rights network's annual review (covering 2023): the national equality body investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; a 2023 survey found 51% of residents agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (a 2018 constitutional referendum to ban them failed on low turnout; church leadership has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBT organisations can register.

A regional human-rights body's thematic review (Jan 2023): a national report on hate crimes and other hate-motivated incidents against LGBTI people — implementation of a 2010 recommendation covering legal and policy frameworks, applicable case-law from the regional human-rights court and international standards.

A rights network's submission to the regional bloc's annual rule-of-law report (2025), with a local rights group authoring the national chapter: of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the national election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
A news outlet (Jun 2025): a gay pride march turned 20 as LGBTQ+ residents faced growing hostility — tens of thousands marched on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

A regional body-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by two legal academics: maps how national law implemented the regional bloc's 2000 employment directive and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, national equality-body enforcement powers and civil-society complaints; a dated baseline for the national protection architecture.
rewrites.notes: Country, cities, courts, persons, organisations, EU/Schengen and church names reduced to generic functions or omitted; the 2024 ruling, March 2026 confirmation, Pride 20th-anniversary and 2024-2025 election-cycle dates retained; verbatim rhetoric quotes paraphrased.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted the prime minister. A trans activist was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having skyrocketed. Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been driven into hiding. A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (a survivor said they escaped only with their life).

Police extort third-gender and trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at the main international airport.

A major foreign government's travel advisory rates the country at Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct is criminalised under a historic-era penal provision (life imprisonment, rarely enforced but used by police for harassment and extortion) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: Third-gender people are legally recognised (2013/2014, a genuine positive), but there is no anti-discrimination law and no comprehensive legal gender recognition — resident-facing framework.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Political instability, mob violence/lynchings, terrorism, and cyclone/monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring group (12 Feb 2025): a prominent trans advocate was murdered in her home on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues.

A monitoring group (7 Apr 2026) citing a national rights federation's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

A news outlet: after the 2024 political upheaval, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; the country has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

A news outlet (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced the prime minister's ouster (August 2024), the country's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

A foreign government's country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026): the historic-era penal provision's ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within it (a 2019 global report on laws read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to all genders). For this record: an authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): the 1860 penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; third-gender people have been legally recognised since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and third-gender pride events have been held. For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

A monitoring group (22 Oct 2025): after third-gender people refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve third-gender people collecting money from vehicles carrying returning expatriates — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

A monitoring group (22 Apr 2024): five transgender women were arrested while begging near the main international airport and sentenced to about a month in custody, per a national rights federation. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

A foreign tribunal decision (Feb 2019): a gay man's asylum appeal — official country material records Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under the historic-era penal provision and religious law, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues. For this record: asylum-grade evidence of official-tolerated hostility; an international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.
rewrites.notes: Place names, persons, outlets and institution names removed; 'hijra' rendered 'third-gender'; colonial-era rendered 'historic-era'; law dates (1860 code, 2013/2014 recognition), the 260/426 counts and 2024-2026 dates retained; quotes paraphrased.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. A 2023 law criminalising same-sex conduct and its promotion imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated" forms, and a major foreign government's travel advisory explicitly warns that the law applies to both visitors and residents. Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes; police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people. The law also criminalises the promotion of such conduct, meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the law targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and official violence. The national constitutional court upheld the law in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

The death penalty applies only to "aggravated" same-sex conduct under this law (not to all same-sex conduct as in some other nations; not to gender expression per se as in others), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic crackdown led by the authorities makes this an environment to avoid entirely.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2023 law's life imprisonment and "aggravated" same-sex death penalty apply to visitors — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app entrapment is a direct app-user risk.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Terrorism (armed groups in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation's report (26 May 2025): the 2023 law — death penalty for aggravated same-sex conduct, lengthy prison terms for promoting such conduct — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

A human-rights organisation (4 Apr 2024): the national constitutional court upheld the 2023 law's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.
Note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (June 2024) covers rights violations against the country's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.

A news outlet (7 Jan 2024): fear across the main city after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false social-media allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a city safe house; notes the death penalty for aggravated same-sex conduct, international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in some other countries.
Note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying foreign-government travel advisory for the country includes LGBT-specific warnings under a 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

A digital-rights organisation (15 May 2025): the country's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device and app risk under the law.

An international rights organisation (23 Oct 2024) report: the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in the country — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the 2023 law fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.
A news outlet (Feb 2026): police arrested two women for allegedly kissing in public — they were detained in a town after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 law.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report for the country: the most important problems included violence and discrimination against marginalised groups — women, children, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community — from the era of the anti-homosexuality bill debates.
rewrites.notes: Country, city, outlet, group and event names removed; the 2023 law's substance and the April 2024 court date retained; statute name reduced to descriptor; the 1,000-violation count and 20-year penalty retained; personal testimony and quotes paraphrased.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by the authorities (a report documenting twelve incidents over 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use vaguely worded morality and cybercrime provisions (six months plus a fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (as documented by a major media investigation) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The interior ministry is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. The country rejected all international recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 periodic human-rights review. The authorities' approach is described as not only to criminalise LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life.

The country has no death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike some other nations), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months plus a fine rather than lengthy prison terms — but the systematic police entrapment, targeting of foreigners, coerced anal examinations, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
rewrites.blindTangential: Dating-app entrapment (documented by a major media investigation) is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps; the morality and cybercrime statutes also capture same-sex conduct.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The gender-affirming healthcare prohibition and the closure of the limited legal gender recognition loophole are resident-facing.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Terrorism (in some border regions), political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.
blindSourceSummaries: A legal-research organisation (27 Nov 2023): analysis of the country's immigration law and case law plus 12 documented incidents (2018-2022) — the interior ministry holds broad powers to deny entry or deport anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', applied to travellers perceived as queer. Directly visitor-facing risk.

A legal-research organisation (24 Jan 2024): the country's economic courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading penal-code provisions together with an article of the 1961 sex-work law; top-court interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the financial-exchange requirement (habitual or multiple partners sufficed).

A legal-research organisation (12 Dec 2024): a new interior-ministry directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closes the 1994 civil-status law loophole that let transgender residents correct gender markers via regional committees — legal gender recognition now actively being shut.

A major media investigation: no explicit law against homosexuality, but the morality (sex-work) law is used to criminalise the community; police run entrapment via dating apps with victims describing blackmail and arrests (names changed).

A local rights group's briefing (Feb 2023): documents rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye, and no anti-discrimination policy or law; covers detention conditions and the situation of trans people as a reference for SOGIESC work.

A rights organisation's security documentation: police arrest patterns — first, entrapment of individuals, especially transgender women, through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites; second, interior-ministry deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld; violations continue inside police stations.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and sex-work laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; no legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

A policy research group (6 Jan 2025): in the country's fourth periodic human-rights review cycle — transgender and intersex residents face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health; barriers to equitable health services persist since the last review, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

A human-rights organisation (29 Feb 2004): documents an early-2000s crackdown — arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants — a landmark record of official violence against gay men in the country.
rewrites.notes: Country, city/region, outlet, app, organisation and event names removed; the 2018-2022 incident count, 2025 review, statutory penalty and law dates retained; study and report titles paraphrased.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is one of the region's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. A comprehensive law for trans people (2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a public-sector employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (the region's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among the region's safest by international safety rankings, with a strong democratic governance structure and a positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties, according to an independent democracy-assessment. However, a 29-year-old trans woman was shot dead in her home in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital and a bank. The assessment notes disparities in treatment for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and the main city is welcoming.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex marriage legal since 2013 (the region's first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The self-declaration legal gender recognition, reparation pension, and public-sector employment quota under the 2018 law are resident-facing; the 2025 killing and the hospital and bank discrimination incidents concerned residents.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBT organisations registrable; intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged incomplete. The current civil-rights baseline a trans visitor enters.

Full text of Law No. 19684 (26 Oct 2018), the nation's comprehensive law for trans people: guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons — the statutory backbone of the country's trans-protection regime.

A legal-status tracking platform's grid for the main city (governed by national law): marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination, conversion-therapy ban and equal age of consent all legal or protected; hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity. Compiled status page, undated.
An official government announcement: the executive promulgated the comprehensive law for trans persons (Oct 2018) — official confirmation the comprehensive trans-rights statute entered into force.
An independent democracy-assessment 2024: Free, 96/100 (political rights 40/40, civil liberties 56/60) — strong general rights climate for trans visitors.

A trans-remembrance project's 2025 record: a 29-year-old trans woman shot dead in her home on 28 Jul 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to 7 years for the murder — documented lethal violence against a trans person with judicial follow-through.

A local news outlet (May 2024): a trans health-service user denounced mistreatment and discrimination at a hospital; a criminal complaint was pending, hospital leadership pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage, and local officials pressed for health-system updates.

A news outlet: a trans woman sued a public bank over discriminatory handling by a security guard and alleged the bank withheld key camera footage; a prosecutor compelled the bank to produce material; she said she was dismissed after publicising the case.

A news outlet (28 Dec 2007): the country became the region's first to recognise same-sex civil unions — the president signed the law giving couples cohabiting 5+ years rights equivalent to marriage (historical baseline).
rewrites.notes: Country, city, persons, outlets, index, platform and bank names removed; law dates (2018, 2013), killing date, sentence, scores and law number retained; 'state' rendered 'public-sector'.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is dangerous for trans visitors. Penal-code provisions dating to 1883 criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and a human-rights organisation lists the country as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and "cheating by personation" provisions against trans people. An international jurists' commission identifies the national police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. The main city has a small organised community and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation or vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.
rewrites.blindTangential: Penal-code provisions criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the vagrancy and "personation" provisions are the trans-specific enforcement vehicle.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The 2016 recognition circular (not law) is a resident-facing instrument.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; legal gender recognition circular limits are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation's country overview (updated March 2026): penal-code provisions criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence — widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).
Note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights organisation's country profile documents the country's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

An international jurists' commission opinion piece (Aug 2023) by a human-rights lawyer: the national police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals; recent months saw both the police and the national human-rights commission acknowledging this; argues administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

A foreign government's country-policy note (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from official and non-official actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

A foreign government's official human-rights country report: assessment including the sexual-orientation and gender-identity section — criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

A joint report by local and international rights groups for the country's periodic human-rights review: documents criminalisation and human-rights violations against LGBTIQ individuals in the country.

An information-request response from a foreign refugee board (Jan 2012): penal-code Article 365 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 10 years, men only); Article 365A covers 'gross indecency' (both sexes, amended 1995 to include women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but the criminalisation paves the way for police and hostile groups to brand lesbian, bisexual and transgender people as deviants.
rewrites.notes: Country, city, persons, outlets and group names removed; penal-code sections, 1883/1995/2016 dates and 10-year penalty retained; quotes paraphrased.
